rationale:
Evidence: all 420 trials across iterations 0-7 ended off track, with exactly one line-loss event per trial and max_error of about 0.061 m. That is just above the 0.06 m off-track limit, which is the floor for any body_width up to 0.18 m. Progress stayed between 0.04 and 0.15. Gain, speed and mass changes moved the score very little (kp 1.5 to 6, kd 0.05 to 0.6, ki 0 to 0.3). Moving the sensors forward (iteration 3) and widening the array to 7 sensors (iteration 4) raised s-bend and slalom progress, so sensing matters. Switching line_loss to search_right (iteration 7) gave a small score gain, but the oval metrics did not move. The near-identical max_error across every design, with a single early line loss, suggests a steady bias rather than oscillation. The fixed left/right motor mismatch is the likely source. Integral action is clamped at +/-2, so ki = 0.3 can only supply about 0.6 of turn, roughly 210 PWM, which may be too small to cancel the mismatch. I have not yet tested a large ki.

Changes: (1) ki raised from 0.05 to 1.0. The integral clamp at 2 gives up to 2 units of turn (about 700 PWM), which tests the mismatch hypothesis directly. (2) Geometry kept from iteration 7 (7 sensors at y = 0.06 m, x = -0.03 to +0.03 m, footprint 0.016 m, mass 0.6 kg, wheel_track 0.14 m) so the only change is the integral term. (3) kp 2.0, kd 0.6, base_speed 1.0 and line_loss search_right unchanged, so the comparison with iteration 7 isolates ki.

Expected result: if a steady mismatch bias is the cause, max_error should fall below 0.06 m and the first line loss should move later or disappear, which would raise progress on the oval and s-bend. If the integral causes overshoot, max_error will rise, which would rule out the bias hypothesis and point to a different cause, such as the start condition or the sensor layout. Finishing within 3 s is still unlikely at this speed.
